  • "Take something to extremes" — very similar in meaning. "She took her passion for fitness to extremes." The slight difference is that "take something to extremes" often focuses on a specific thing being pushed too far, while "go to extremes" can describe a person's general tendency.
  • "Go overboard" — means to do too much of something, very close in meaning. "He went overboard with the decorations." It's slightly more informal and often used humorously.
  • "Go too far" — means to cross a line, to do something beyond acceptable limits. "That joke went too far." This often implies crossing a moral or social boundary, whereas "go to extremes" focuses more on intensity or excess.
  • "In the extreme" — this is a different phrase meaning "to a very great degree." "The situation was dangerous in the extreme." Don't confuse it with "go to extremes."
  • "Extremism" — the noun form of the same idea applied to politics, religion, or ideology. When beliefs "go to extremes," they can become extremism.

It's worth clarifying a few things this idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean going to an extreme location (like an extreme sport setting or an extreme climate). It is purely about behavior, attitude, or degree — not physical places.
  • It does not always mean something is wrong. Context decides whether excess is being criticized or admired.
  • It is not the same as simply "doing a lot." Doing a lot of something is normal effort. Going to extremes means pushing well past the reasonable limit.
A Simple Way to Remember It Forever

Picture a tightrope walker. The safe, balanced position is in the middle of the rope. Most sensible people stay near the center. Someone who "goes to extremes" runs to the very end of the rope — or even leaps off it entirely. They abandon balance and moderation and go as far as things can possibly go.

If "balance" is the opposite of "going to extremes," then you'll never forget what this idiom means.

MeaningTo do something in an excessive, exaggerated, or overly intense way; to lack moderation
ToneUsually mildly negative (critical); sometimes neutral or admiring
Used forBehaviors, opinions, emotions, plans, decisions
Key ideaSkipping the middle ground and going all the way to the furthest point
6944:
When someone "goes to great lengths" to do something, it means they try extremely hard and are willing to put in a lot of effort, time, energy, or resources to achieve a goal — often more than what is normally expected.

The key idea is that the person does not take the easy route. They push themselves far beyond the ordinary, doing whatever it takes.

Think of it this way: imagine effort on a scale from 1 to 10. Most people operate at a 5 or 6. Someone who "goes to great lengths" is at a 9 or 10.
Breaking Down the Words

To really understand an idiom, it helps to look at the individual words — even though idioms don't always mean what the words literally say.

"Length" in English can mean distance, but it can also mean the degree or extent to which something is done. So "great lengths" = a great extent, a high degree of effort.

"Go to" here means to reach a certain point, or to go as far as something requires.

Put it together: "Go to great lengths" = to extend your efforts to a very great degree. You are "travelling far" — not physically, but in terms of how much you are willing to do.
The Feeling Behind It

This idiom carries a strong sense of dedication, determination, and sometimes even sacrifice. It often signals that:

  • The goal matters a lot to the person.
  • They are not lazy or casual about it.
  • They went beyond what is normal or comfortable.

The tone can be admiring ("Wow, she really worked hard!") or sometimes critical ("He's obsessed — he went too far"). Context tells you which one it is.
Everyday Examples

Here are clear, simple examples that show how the idiom is used in real life:

Example 1 (Positive/Admiring):
"She goes to great lengths to make sure her students understand the lesson — she creates extra worksheets, stays after class, and even calls parents to check in."
→ She puts in a huge amount of effort for her students.

Example 2 (Parenting):
"Parents often go to great lengths to give their children the best possible life."
→ Parents are willing to sacrifice and work hard for their kids.

Example 3 (Business):
"The company went to great lengths to keep the product launch a secret."
→ They did many things — perhaps unusual or difficult things — to maintain secrecy.

Example 4 (Slightly Critical):
"He goes to great lengths to avoid his neighbor — he even takes a longer route to work every day!"
→ Here, the effort seems a bit extreme or funny. The tone is slightly humorous or critical.

Example 5 (Historical/News):
"The government went to great lengths to protect the identity of the witness."
→ They used serious, extensive measures.
How to Use It Grammatically

The structure is almost always:

[Someone] + go/goes/went to great lengths + to + [verb]

  • She goes to great lengths to impress her boss.
  • They went to great lengths to find the missing child.
  • He will go to great lengths to protect his family.
  • The team went to great lengths to ensure accuracy.

The phrase is always followed by "to + a verb" that tells you what the person is trying to achieve. The idiom rarely stands alone without this explanation of the goal.
Variations You Will Hear

The core idiom has some close relatives that mean nearly the same thing:

"Go to any length(s)"
This means the person is willing to do absolutely anything, with no limit. It's even stronger.
"She will go to any length to protect her children."

"Go to extreme lengths"
This emphasizes how unusual or excessive the effort is.
"He went to extreme lengths to win the competition."

"Go to extraordinary lengths"
This is often used to express admiration at how impressive the effort was.
"The rescue team went to extraordinary lengths to save the hikers."
Similar Expressions (Same Meaning)

These idioms and phrases carry a very similar meaning and can often replace "go to great lengths":

  • "Move heaven and earth" — to do everything possible, no matter how hard.

"She moved heaven and earth to get her visa approved in time."

  • "Leave no stone unturned" — to try every possible option or solution.

"The detective left no stone unturned in the investigation."

  • "Bend over backwards" — to try very hard to help or please someone.

"The staff bent over backwards to make the guests comfortable."

  • "Pull out all the stops" — to use every resource or effort available.

"They pulled out all the stops for the grand opening."

  • "Do everything in one's power" — to use all of one's ability.

"He did everything in his power to save the business."
Opposite Expressions

Just as useful as knowing the idiom is knowing what the opposite looks like:

  • "Half-hearted effort" — trying, but not really caring or pushing hard.
  • "Cut corners" — doing something the easy, lazy, or cheap way.
  • "Do the bare minimum" — doing only what is absolutely necessary, nothing more.
  • "Go through the motions" — doing something without real effort or sincerity.
Formal or Informal?

This idiom fits comfortably in both formal and informal contexts. You can use it in:

  • A professional email or report: "Our team went to great lengths to ensure the data was accurate."
  • A casual conversation: "She literally went to great lengths to bake that birthday cake for you — she ordered ingredients from three different stores!"
  • News articles, essays, speeches, and books.

It is not rude, slang, or offensive in any way, making it a very safe and versatile expression.
A Common Mistake to Avoid

Learners sometimes say "go to a great length" (singular). While not terribly wrong, the far more natural and accepted form is always the plural: "great lengths." Always use the plural.

❌ "He went to a great length to help me." (Unusual)
✅ "He went to great lengths to help me." (Correct and natural)
Quick Summary

MeaningTo put in a very high level of effort to achieve something
ToneUsually admiring; sometimes critical if the effort is excessive
Structure[Someone] + go to great lengths + to + [verb]
FormalityBoth formal and informal
Key feelingDedication, determination, going beyond the ordinary

In short, whenever you see or hear "go to great lengths," picture someone who cares so much about a goal that they are willing to travel the full distance — putting in extraordinary effort to make it happen. That image will never let you forget this idiom.
6945:
"Go to pot" means to deteriorate, decline, or fall into a state of ruin or neglect. When something or someone "goes to pot," it means they were once good, healthy, or well-functioning, but over time — usually due to neglect, misuse, or lack of care — they have become worse, weaker, or a shadow of what they used to be.

Think of it this way: imagine a beautiful garden. It has colourful flowers, trimmed hedges, and clean paths. Then, the owner stops caring for it. Weeds take over. Flowers die. The paths crack. That garden has gone to pot.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

This is one of the oldest idioms in the English language, dating back to at least the 16th century.

The most widely accepted origin comes from the kitchen. In the old days, when a piece of meat or food was no longer fresh or good enough to be served as a proper meal, it was thrown into a large cooking pot to be boiled down into a stew or broth — basically, it became scraps. So something that "went to the pot" was something that had lost its prime value and been reduced to its lowest form.

Another related theory involves metalwork. Broken or worn-out metal objects — tools, coins, ornaments — were thrown into a melting pot to be melted down and recycled. The object essentially lost its identity, its purpose, and its value. It was gone.

Both origins share the same central idea: something that was once useful and valuable has been reduced to nothing.
The Core Feeling of This Idiom

This idiom always carries a sense of sadness, disappointment, or regret. There is always a contrast between a better past and a worse present. The thing that has gone to pot was not always bad — it used to be good. That is what makes the phrase feel melancholic.
What Can "Go to Pot"?

This idiom is very flexible. It can be used for almost anything:

A place:
"This neighbourhood used to be safe and lively. It's really gone to pot over the last ten years."

A person's health or appearance:
"He was a brilliant, energetic professor, but after his illness, he went to pot completely."

A person's career or skills:
"She was one of the best pianists in the country, but after she stopped practising, her talent went to pot."

A relationship:
"Their friendship went to pot after that argument — they never spoke again."

An organisation or team:
"The company went to pot after the original founders left."

A plan or project:
"We had a strong strategy, but without proper leadership, the whole thing went to pot."

A habit or routine:
"My fitness routine has really gone to pot since I started working extra hours."
The Tone and Register

This is an informal, conversational idiom. You would use it when speaking or writing casually — with friends, family, or in an informal piece of writing. You would generally avoid it in formal essays, official reports, or professional business communication, where it might sound too casual or colloquial.
Active vs. Passive Use

You can use this idiom in two ways:

Active (someone caused the decline):
"Neglect and poor management let the business go to pot."

Passive / natural decline (no one specific is to blame):
"The old library has gone to pot over the decades."

Both are correct. The idiom works whether the decline was caused by someone's fault or simply happened on its own over time.
Tense and Form

The idiom is almost always used in the past tense or present perfect, because it describes something that has already declined. You rarely say something will go to pot — though it is possible.

Common forms:

  • "It has gone to pot." ✅ (most common)
  • "It went to pot." ✅
  • "Things are going to pot." ✅ (ongoing decline)
  • "It will go to pot if nothing changes." ✅ (future warning)
Similar Idioms and Expressions

Understanding related expressions will sharpen your grasp of this one:

"Go to the dogs" — very similar in meaning; a decline in quality or standards. Slightly stronger in tone.
"This city has really gone to the dogs."

"Go downhill" — to gradually get worse over time.
"His health has been going downhill since last year."

"Go to rack and ruin" — to fall into a state of complete neglect and destruction, often used for buildings or physical places.
"The old castle has gone to rack and ruin."

"Go to seed" — to decline after having been at a peak; often used for people who have let themselves go physically.
"He was quite handsome in his youth, but he's gone to seed."

"Fall apart" — to stop functioning properly; less poetic, more direct.
"Their marriage just fell apart."

Among these, "go to pot" is perhaps the most general and the most commonly used for a broad range of subjects.
What "Go to Pot" Does NOT Mean

A quick note to avoid confusion: in modern slang, "pot" is sometimes used as an informal word for cannabis/marijuana. The idiom "go to pot" has absolutely nothing to do with that meaning. They are completely unrelated. The idiom is centuries older and comes from the kitchen/metallurgy meaning described above.
A Quick Summary

Core meaningTo deteriorate or decline from a formerly good state
CauseNeglect, misuse, lack of care, or simply time
ToneInformal, slightly sad or disappointed
Used forPeople, places, organisations, relationships, skills, plans
RegisterCasual/conversational — avoid in formal writing
One Final Example to Tie It All Together

Imagine a sports team. Ten years ago, they won championships every season. The stadium was packed. The players were disciplined and talented. Then, the manager left, the funding dried up, and the best players moved to other teams. Nobody trained properly. They began losing every match. The stadium is now half-empty.

You would say: "That team has really gone to pot."

That sentence, in just five words, tells the whole story — there was a glorious past, and now there is a sad, neglected present.
6946:
To truly understand this idiom, you first need to understand what actually happens to a plant in a garden.

A plant goes through a life cycle. First, it grows strong and healthy. Then, it blooms — producing beautiful flowers or fresh, lush leaves. This is the plant at its peak. It looks vibrant, attractive, and full of life.

But after that peak, something changes. The plant stops putting energy into looking beautiful. Instead, it shifts all its energy toward one final job: producing seeds so that new plants can grow after it dies. The flowers wither and dry up. The leaves turn dull and yellow. The stems become thin, straggly, and untidy. The whole plant starts to look neglected, overgrown, and past its best days.

This process is called "going to seed." A gardener who sees this happening knows the plant has passed its prime and is now in a state of decline and neglect.

When we use "go to seed" as an idiom in everyday language, we borrow that exact image from the garden and apply it to people, places, or things that were once in good condition but have since deteriorated, declined, or become neglected.

In simple words: something or someone that was once impressive, well-kept, or at their best has now fallen into a poor, shabby, or neglected state.

The key idea is always:

  • There was a former time of quality or good condition.
  • That time has passed.
  • Now there is noticeable decline or neglect.
Who or What Can "Go to Seed"?

This idiom is flexible. It can be used in three main ways:

1. A Person

This is the most common use. When a person "goes to seed," they have stopped taking care of themselves — physically, mentally, or professionally — after previously being in good shape or at the top of their game.

Examples:

  • "He was a sharp, energetic businessman in his 40s, but after he retired, he really went to seed. He stopped exercising, gave up his hobbies, and lost all his drive."
  • "She used to be so fit and disciplined, but ever since she quit the team, she's gone to seed."

It can refer to physical appearance (gaining weight, looking unkempt), mental sharpness (losing focus or ambition), or overall personal standards (not caring about hygiene, dress, or behavior).

2. A Place

A building, a neighborhood, a garden, or any location that was once well-maintained but has now become run-down, dirty, or neglected.

Examples:

  • "This neighborhood used to be so charming in the 1980s, but it's really gone to seed — broken windows, overgrown yards, crumbling walls everywhere."
  • "The old estate has gone to seed. The gardens are wild and the house is falling apart."

3. A Thing, Organization, or Institution

A company, a tradition, a system, or anything that once had quality or prestige but has now declined.

Examples:

  • "That magazine used to publish brilliant writing, but it's gone to seed — the articles are shallow and poorly edited now."
  • "The once-great football club has gone to seed since the legendary coach left."
The Tone and Feeling of This Idiom

This is important to understand so you use it correctly.

"Go to seed" carries a tone of mild sadness or disappointment — not angry criticism. It suggests a slow, gradual decline over time, not a sudden failure. There is often a sense of nostalgia in it — a quiet regret that something or someone that was once good is no longer what it used to be.

It is not an extremely harsh or insulting phrase, but it is definitely negative. You would not say it to someone's face without risking offending them. It's the kind of thing people say when describing something or someone who isn't present, or when observing a place from the outside.
The Most Common Form: "Gone to Seed"

You will most often hear this idiom in the past tense: "gone to seed." This makes sense because the idiom describes a completed process of decline — the deterioration has already happened.

  • "This town has really gone to seed." ✅ (most common)
  • "He's starting to go to seed." ✅ (decline is just beginning)
  • "The garden was going to seed." ✅ (decline was in progress)

You may sometimes hear the variation "run to seed." It means exactly the same thing. This version is slightly more common in British English, while "go to seed" is widely used in both British and American English.

  • "The old hotel has run to seed since the new owners took over."

Treat them as interchangeable.

Picture a once-beautiful rose bush in a garden. In spring, it was stunning — full of bright red roses, neatly trimmed, admired by everyone who walked past. But then the owner stopped caring for it. By autumn, the roses are gone, replaced by dry, stringy seed pods. The bush is tangled, dull, and scraggly. It has gone to seed.

Now replace that rose bush with a person, a building, or an organization — and you have the idiom perfectly.

AspectDetail

"Go to seed" means to decline or deteriorate from a previously good condition, due to neglect or the simple passage of time. It comes from the natural process of a plant moving past its flowering peak and becoming overgrown and scraggly. It is used for people (who let themselves go), places (that become run-down), and things or organizations (that lose their former quality). The tone is one of mild sadness or disappointment. The past tense — "gone to seed" — is the most common form. "Run to seed" is an equally valid variant.
6947:
Imagine being in a fight and getting pushed so far back that your back literally hits the wall behind you. You have nowhere left to go. You are completely trapped, defeated, with no options remaining.

That physical image is the heart of this idiom. "Go to the wall" captures the idea of reaching an extreme endpoint — either total failure, or total commitment.

This idiom has two distinct meanings, and knowing both is essential because they can look like opposites at first glance.

Meaning 1: To Fail Completely (Most Common, Especially in Business)

When a person, business, or organisation "goes to the wall," it means they have collapsed, failed, or been destroyed — usually financially or competitively.

Think of it like a boxing match. The loser gets pushed back and back until they hit the wall of the ring. They can't retreat any further. They've lost. That is "going to the wall."

Examples:

  • "Dozens of small shops went to the wall when the big supermarket opened nearby."
  • "The startup went to the wall after it ran out of funding."
  • "Many banks went to the wall during the financial crisis."

Key point: In this meaning, going to the wall is something that happens to a person or organisation. It is done to them by circumstances, competition, or bad luck. It is almost always a negative outcome.

This is the primary meaning in British English, and you will see it constantly in news articles about business failures, economic downturns, or competitive industries.

Meaning 2: To Support Someone Fully, No Matter What

In this second meaning, "go to the wall for someone" means to fight as hard as possible for a person, to defend them completely, and to be willing to sacrifice yourself for them. It means your loyalty and effort have no limits.

Here, the "wall" represents the absolute furthest you are willing to go. You will fight until your back is literally against the wall — until you have nothing left to give — before you stop defending that person.

Examples:

  • "She would go to the wall for her children — nothing would stop her from protecting them."
  • "He is the kind of manager who goes to the wall for his team when the company tries to cut their budget."
  • "I know she'll go to the wall for me — she's the most loyal friend I've ever had."

Key point: In this meaning, going to the wall is something you choose to do actively. It shows great loyalty, courage, and selflessness. It is always a positive quality in the person doing it.
How to Tell the Two Meanings Apart

The grammar will almost always make it clear:

  • "go to the wall" (no object) = to fail, to collapse.

"The business went to the wall."

  • "go to the wall for someone" (with "for" + a person) = to support someone completely.

"She went to the wall for her colleague."

Whenever you see the word "for" followed by a person, you are almost certainly looking at the second meaning — loyalty and sacrifice.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

The origin of this idiom goes back several centuries, and there are two well-supported historical explanations.

1. Medieval churches had no seats.
In the Middle Ages, ordinary people stood during church services — there were no pews or chairs. The only relief available was a narrow stone bench built along the walls of the church. Only the weakest, oldest, or most unwell members of the congregation were allowed to go and rest against the wall. Everyone else had to stand. This gave rise to the old saying "the weakest go to the wall," meaning that those who cannot keep up with the strong are forced aside. Over time, this evolved into the general idea of failing or being pushed out by forces stronger than yourself.

2. Being cornered in battle or conflict.
Throughout history, being driven back against a wall in any kind of fight — a street brawl, a military battle, or a duel — meant total defeat. When you hit the wall, you had no room left to manoeuvre. You were finished. This physical image of being backed into a wall naturally became a metaphor for any kind of complete, final failure or defeat.

Both of these origins feed into the modern meanings of the idiom. The image of the wall as the absolute endpoint — the place you reach when everything else has run out — runs through both of them.
Register and Usage — When and Where People Use It

• This idiom is widely used in everyday English, particularly in British English.
  • It appears frequently in journalism and business writing (Meaning 1) and in personal conversation (Meaning 2).
  • It is not slang — it is completely appropriate in formal writing, journalism, academic essays, and professional speech, as well as in casual conversation.
  • It is more common in British English than American English, though American speakers understand and use it too.

Mistake 1: Confusing the two meanings.
Because one meaning is about failure and the other is about loyalty, mixing them up changes your sentence entirely. Always check whether "for + a person" follows the phrase.

Mistake 2: Using it for small, minor setbacks.
"Going to the wall" implies something total and extreme. You wouldn't say someone "went to the wall" because they lost a small argument or faced a minor inconvenience. The failure must be serious — a business shutting down, a career collapsing, a defeat with no recovery. Similarly, the loyalty must be deep and unconditional, not just mild support.

Mistake 3: Thinking it only applies to money or business.
While business failure is the most common use of Meaning 1, the idiom can apply to any kind of complete defeat — a political party, a sports club, a relationship, or even an idea.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

"Go to the wall" means one of two things:

  1. To completely fail or collapse — used especially for businesses, organisations, or ambitions that are destroyed by competition, debt, or circumstance. (Something that happens to you.)
  2. To support someone with total loyalty, even at great personal cost — used to describe someone who would sacrifice everything for another person. (Something you actively choose to do.)

The unifying thread in both meanings is the image of reaching the absolute limit — the wall behind you, with nowhere left to go. In one case, that limit is your ruin. In the other, it is a measure of how far your devotion will reach.
6948:
"Go under" is a phrasal verb — a two-word verb made by combining a common verb ("go") with a preposition or adverb ("under"). Phrasal verbs are extremely common in English, and the same phrasal verb can have several very different meanings depending on the situation. "Go under" is a perfect example of this. It has four core meanings, all of which you need to know.

The good news is that all four meanings share a single underlying logic. Once you understand that logic, everything clicks into place.
The Core Idea Behind All Meanings

Think about what literally happens when something "goes under" water. It sinks. It disappears from view. It stops functioning on the surface. It is overwhelmed by something bigger than itself.

Every meaning of "go under" connects back to this image — something being submerged, overwhelmed, hidden, or losing its fight against a force greater than it.
Meaning 1: To Sink Beneath the Surface (Literal)

This is the original, physical meaning of the phrase. When something goes under, it sinks below the surface of a liquid — most commonly water — and disappears.

Examples:

  • "The old fishing boat took on too much water and slowly went under."
  • "She slipped off the rock and went under, but her friend quickly pulled her out."
  • "The rescuers watched helplessly as the car went under the flooded river."

This meaning is almost always used with water or another liquid as the implied surface. It describes the actual physical act of sinking or going below that surface. Notice that the word "under" here is literal — the thing is physically going under something.
Meaning 2: To Go Bankrupt / To Fail (Business)

This is the most common figurative use of "go under," and it is used very frequently in everyday English. When a business, company, or organization "goes under," it means it has failed financially — it ran out of money, could not pay its debts, and had to close down permanently.

Think of it this way: just as a boat sinks and disappears beneath the water when it can no longer stay afloat, a business "goes under" when it can no longer stay financially afloat. The metaphor is borrowed directly from Meaning 1.

Examples:

  • "The restaurant went under after just six months because it had very few customers."
  • "Dozens of small shops went under during the economic crisis."
  • "If we don't get more investors soon, this startup will go under."
  • "Everyone was shocked when the hundred-year-old bank went under overnight."

This is an informal but widely accepted way of saying a business has become insolvent or bankrupt. You will hear this in everyday conversation, in news reports, and in business discussions. It works for any kind of organization — a shop, a company, a bank, a restaurant, even a school.

Note: You can also extend this meaning slightly beyond business. If a person "goes under" in a broader struggle — like being buried in debt or overwhelmed by responsibilities — you can use this phrase for them too, though the business meaning is by far the most common.
Meaning 3: To Lose Consciousness / To Go Under Anesthesia

When a person undergoes surgery or a medical procedure, they are often given anesthesia — a substance that puts them into a deep, unconscious sleep so they feel no pain. The moment they lose consciousness is described as "going under."

The logic is again connected to the original water image. When you are unconscious, you are not "on the surface" of the world — you have sunk into a deep, dark state where you are unaware of everything around you.

Examples:

  • "The doctor told her to count backwards from ten, and she went under before she reached seven."
  • "He was nervous about going under for the first time in his life."
  • "The anesthetic took effect quickly, and the patient went under in less than a minute."
  • "She doesn't remember anything because she went under before the procedure even started."

This usage is almost exclusively tied to anesthesia and medical procedures. If you hear someone say "she went under" in a hospital context, this is almost certainly what they mean. Doctors, nurses, and patients all use this phrase routinely.
Meaning 4: To Be Known By / To Use a Particular Name (Identity)

This meaning is a little different from the others, but it still carries the idea of something being hidden or not fully visible. When someone "goes under" a name, alias, or title, it means they use that particular name — often a fake name, a nickname, a stage name, or a professional name — instead of their real one.

The idea here is that their true identity is "beneath the surface," hidden under a different name.

Examples:

  • "The spy went under the name 'Victor' while on his mission."
  • "She goes under the stage name 'Luna' for all her performances."
  • "The author goes under a pen name because she wants to keep her identity private."
  • "He was known to the police and went under at least three different aliases."

You will notice that this meaning always requires an additional element — the name itself. The structure is always: go under + a name / an alias / a title. Without a name following it, this meaning does not work.
A Quick Summary of the Four Meanings (In Plain Words)

To sink below the surface of water or liquid — this is the literal, physical meaning. To collapse and fail completely, especially in a financial sense — this is the most common everyday figurative meaning. To become unconscious, particularly from anesthesia — this is the medical meaning. To use a particular name or identity, often one that hides who you really are — this is the identity-related meaning.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Context is everything with phrasal verbs, and "go under" is no exception. Here is how to quickly figure out which meaning applies:

If the sentence is about water, a river, a flood, or anything physical sinking — it is Meaning 1 (literal sinking).

If the sentence is about a business, a company, a shop, or money — it is Meaning 2 (business failure).

If the sentence is about a hospital, surgery, an operation, or a doctor — it is Meaning 3 (losing consciousness).

If the sentence includes a name, a title, or an alias directly after "go under" — it is Meaning 4 (using an identity/name).

"Go under" is informal to neutral in tone. It is perfectly fine to use it in casual conversation, but it is also acceptable in writing. The business meaning (Meaning 2) in particular appears regularly in news articles and reports.

It is not a rude, vulgar, or overly formal phrase. It sits comfortably in everyday English.
One Final Trick to Remember Everything

Picture a ship. When a ship is functioning and healthy, it stays on the surface. When it fails — when it is overwhelmed by water, by damage, by forces too powerful for it — it goes under. It sinks. It disappears. It is no longer visible on the surface.

That same image applies to all four meanings. A drowning person goes under the water. A failing business goes under when it cannot stay afloat financially. A surgery patient goes under when they sink into unconsciousness. A person going under a false name has their real self hidden beneath the surface of a different identity.

Everything is connected to the same root image: something overwhelmed, submerged, or hidden beneath what is visible on the surface.
6949:
A go-ahead is an official or informal permission given by someone in authority that allows a person, group, or project to start or continue moving forward with something.

Think of it like a green traffic light. You are at a red light — your car is ready, your engine is running, but you cannot move yet. The moment the light turns green, you have your "go-ahead." That green light is the signal that says: "Yes, you may proceed now."

The go-ahead is exactly that — the signal, the approval, the clearance that removes the obstacle between waiting and acting.
Why Was There Waiting in the First Place?

This is important to understand. A go-ahead doesn't exist in isolation. It always comes after a period of pause, uncertainty, or dependence on someone else's decision. Something — a plan, a project, an action — is ready and waiting, but it cannot begin or continue until a decision-maker says yes.

That decision, when it finally comes, is the go-ahead.

The go-ahead is always given by someone who has the authority or power to approve or block the action. This could be:

  • A boss or manager approving a business plan
  • A government body approving a construction project
  • A doctor clearing a patient to return to physical activity
  • A parent allowing a child to do something
  • A commander authorizing an operation

The key is that without this person's approval, things cannot and do not move forward.
The Most Common Phrases You Will See

The word "go-ahead" as a noun almost always appears with these verbs:

  • Give the go-ahead — the authority figure approves it.
    "The mayor gave the go-ahead for the new bridge."
  • Get / receive the go-ahead — the waiting party receives the approval.
    "We finally got the go-ahead from the investors."
  • Await the go-ahead — to be in that state of waiting for permission.
    "The team is awaiting the go-ahead to begin drilling."
  • Grant the go-ahead — a slightly more formal way of saying "give."
    "The committee granted the go-ahead for the clinical trial."

Notice that it almost always appears as "the go-ahead" — with the word the in front of it — because it refers to one specific, concrete act of permission for one specific purpose.

In business:
"After months of planning and review, the board of directors finally gave the go-ahead to launch the new product."
→ The product was ready. The team was ready. They just needed the board's blessing to move.

In medicine:
"The surgeon gave the patient the go-ahead to start light exercise six weeks after the operation."
→ The patient had been recovering and waiting. The doctor's clearance — the go-ahead — meant it was now safe to act.

In construction and government:
"Environmental inspectors gave the go-ahead for the factory to resume operations after the safety checks were complete."
→ The factory was shut down, waiting. The inspectors' approval was the go-ahead.

In everyday life:
"My manager gave me the go-ahead to work from home for the rest of the month."
→ A simple, informal permission — but still a go-ahead.
What Makes "Go-Ahead" Different from Just Saying "Permission"?

This is a subtle but important distinction.

The word permission is broad. You can have permission to do something in a general, ongoing sense — like having permission to use someone's Wi-Fi whenever you want.

A go-ahead, however, is almost always tied to a specific action, project, or plan that is ready and waiting to be set in motion. It carries a strong sense of forward movement and momentum. When a go-ahead is given, things start happening. It is the moment that unlocks action.

It also tends to feel slightly more official or significant than simple, casual permission. A go-ahead is often the result of a deliberation, review, or decision-making process — not just a casual "sure, go ahead."

When people talk about waiting for a go-ahead, there is often a sense of eagerness, tension, or anticipation. Something important is on hold. A go-ahead is therefore not just a bureaucratic detail — it is often a turning point, the moment everything changes from standstill to action.

This is why the word is used so often in high-stakes contexts: major construction projects, medical decisions, business launches, military operations. The go-ahead is the moment the waiting ends and the doing begins.

What it isA specific permission or approval that allows something to begin or continue
Who gives itSomeone with authority over the decision
When it's usedWhen something is on hold and needs approval to move forward
Key feelingRelief, momentum, a turning point from waiting to acting

In one sentence: The go-ahead is the green light from someone in authority that finally allows a waiting plan, project, or action to move forward.
6950:
A go-between is a person who sits in the middle of two other parties and helps them communicate, exchange information, or reach an agreement — especially when those two parties are not talking to each other directly, or simply find it difficult or uncomfortable to do so.

Think of it like a human bridge. On one side, you have Person A. On the other side, you have Person B. They need something to pass between them — a message, an offer, a piece of news, a negotiation. The go-between is the person who walks back and forth across that bridge, carrying things from one side to the other.

The key features of a go-between are:

1. There are always two separate parties involved.
A go-between never works for just one side. Their entire purpose depends on the existence of two parties who need to be connected. Remove either party, and the role disappears.

2. The two parties are not communicating directly.
This is the whole reason a go-between exists. Maybe the two sides are hostile toward each other. Maybe they are too shy or embarrassed. Maybe there are rules or social norms preventing direct contact. Maybe the distance — physical, emotional, or cultural — makes direct contact difficult. Whatever the reason, the go-between fills that gap.

3. The go-between carries something between the two sides.
This could be words, messages, offers, proposals, demands, gifts, information, or even money. The go-between is essentially a carrier or courier of communication.

4. The go-between often has the trust of both sides.
This is what makes them effective. If only one side trusted them, they wouldn't be able to work with the other. A good go-between has a foot in both worlds.

Example 1 — A family dispute:
Two brothers had a bitter argument years ago and haven't spoken since. Their sister stays in touch with both of them. When the family home needs to be sold, she passes messages between the two brothers, relays each one's position to the other, and helps them reach a decision — without them ever having to speak directly. She is the go-between.

Example 2 — A workplace situation:
A junior employee wants to raise a sensitive concern with the CEO, but feels too nervous to approach them directly. A senior manager who knows both parties agrees to communicate the concern on the employee's behalf and bring back the CEO's response. That senior manager is acting as a go-between.

Example 3 — A romantic situation:
In many cultures or stories, a young person uses a mutual friend to pass a love letter to someone they admire. That mutual friend — who delivers the letter and brings back a reply — is the go-between.

Example 4 — International diplomacy:
Two countries refuse to sit at the same table because of a political conflict. A third, neutral country sends its representatives to travel between the two capitals, carrying each side's proposals to the other and working toward a peace agreement. Those representatives are acting as go-betweens on a grand scale.

The word go-between is mostly neutral — it simply describes a role or function, without judging whether the role is good or bad. However, context can color it in different ways:

  • In professional or diplomatic settings, being a go-between is often a respected role. Skilled negotiators and mediators are proud to serve in this capacity. It requires tact, trust, and communication skills.
  • In personal or secretive situations, the word can sometimes carry a slightly sneaky or delicate feeling — for example, if someone is acting as a go-between in a secret romance or in backroom negotiations that aren't fully transparent.
  • Occasionally, a go-between can be manipulative — someone who exploits their middle position to serve their own interests, telling each side what they want to hear rather than the truth. In such cases, the word takes on a negative feeling.

But none of these negative possibilities are built into the word itself. The neutral core meaning is simply: a person who facilitates communication between two parties who are not in direct contact.
How It Differs From Similar Words

It helps to see how "go-between" sits alongside related concepts:

A messenger simply carries a message from A to B. They don't necessarily go back and forth, and they are not expected to negotiate or mediate — just deliver.

A mediator is more active — they try to resolve a conflict, often guiding both sides toward a solution, sometimes even suggesting compromises. A go-between can do this, but doesn't have to.

An intermediary is a more formal, often business or legal word for essentially the same concept as a go-between — a middle party who connects two other parties.

A broker facilitates a specific transaction — a deal, a sale, a contract. A real estate agent, for example, is a broker between a buyer and a seller.

Of all these, go-between is the broadest and most human-centered. It emphasizes the back-and-forth movement between two sides, and it is used for a wide range of situations — personal, social, professional, and political.

If you had to remember just one thing: a go-between is a person who passes communication between two parties who are not talking to each other directly, acting as the link that keeps things moving between them.
6951:
A go-getter is a person who is highly ambitious, energetic, and driven to achieve their goals. The key idea is that they don't sit around waiting for good things to happen to them — they actively go out and make things happen. They take charge of their own success.

The word essentially captures this spirit in its very structure: a person who "goes and gets" what they want, instead of hoping it will land in their lap.
The deeper picture — what truly defines a go-getter

A go-getter is not simply a hard worker. Plenty of people work hard but only do exactly what they are told. A go-getter goes further than that. They show initiative, meaning they act on their own without waiting for instructions or permission. They see what needs to be done, and they do it — sometimes before anyone else even realizes it needs doing.

A go-getter also has a strong sense of purpose and direction. They know what they want, and they pursue it with focus and determination. Obstacles don't stop them easily; setbacks might slow them down, but they find ways around problems rather than giving up.

Another important quality is proactiveness. Where an ordinary person reacts to situations as they come, a go-getter looks ahead, spots opportunities early, and moves toward them before others even notice. They create their own chances rather than waiting for luck.
The feeling the word carries (its connotation)

"Go-getter" is a very positive word. When someone calls you a go-getter, it is a genuine compliment. It means they respect your drive, your ambition, and your energy. It signals that you are someone who gets results, who can be counted on, and who brings enthusiasm to everything they do.

You will almost never hear this word used in a negative or sarcastic way in normal conversation. It is the kind of word a proud parent uses to describe their child, or a manager uses to praise a star employee.
Where and when you'll encounter this word

"Go-getter" is used mostly in professional, career, and personal development contexts. You'll see it in job descriptions ("We're looking for a go-getter to join our sales team"), in performance reviews, in motivational writing, and in everyday conversation when people talk about someone they admire for their drive.

It can describe people of any age — a teenager who starts their own small business, a young professional who volunteers for every new project, or an entrepreneur who builds a company from scratch despite every difficulty.

"Even as a student, she was a go-getter — she always finished her assignments early and started the next ones without being asked."

"We need go-getters on this team, not people who wait around to be told what to do."

"His reputation as a go-getter got him promoted faster than anyone in the company's history."

"If you want to succeed in a competitive field like this, you have to be a go-getter."
What a go-getter is NOT — important distinctions

It is worth clearing up a few possible confusions.

A go-getter is not someone who is pushy, rude, or steps on others to get ahead. The word does not carry that meaning. A go-getter is driven and ambitious, but in a way that earns respect, not resentment.

A go-getter is also not just someone who is busy or works long hours. Busyness without direction is not what this word means. A go-getter is busy with purpose — chasing specific goals with intention.

Finally, a go-getter is not merely someone who is talented or gifted. Natural talent is separate. A go-getter is defined by their attitude and behavior — their will to pursue, to initiate, to persist — not simply by what they are born with.
Words that are close in meaning

The nearest synonym is self-starter, which emphasizes the same idea of taking initiative without needing to be pushed. High achiever is similar but focuses more on the results (what they accomplish) rather than the attitude. Driven individual or ambitious person are also close. Dynamo is a more informal, energetic-sounding equivalent. Among all of these, "go-getter" stands out because it beautifully captures both the energy and the ambition in a single, vivid word.

A go-getter is someone who combines ambition, initiative, energy, and determination to actively pursue their goals — a person who goes out and gets what they want rather than waiting for it to come to them, and who is genuinely admired for that quality.
6952:
A go-slow is a form of protest by workers in which they deliberately do their jobs at a much slower pace than usual — but without stopping work entirely. Instead of walking off the job (which would be a strike), workers show up, clock in, and do their tasks, but they drag their feet on purpose. Everything moves at a crawl. The goal is to frustrate the employer and cut down on productivity until demands are met.

Think of it this way: imagine a factory that normally produces 500 units a day. During a go-slow, the same workers might produce only 150 units — not because they can't do more, but because they've collectively agreed not to.

Workers usually want something — higher wages, better working conditions, fewer working hours, safer environments, or fairer treatment. When employers refuse to listen or negotiate, workers need a way to apply pressure.

A go-slow sits right in the middle ground between two extremes:

  • On one end is normal work — showing up and doing your full job.
  • On the other end is a strike — refusing to work at all.

A go-slow is a deliberate strategy that lives between these two. Workers keep earning their wages (unlike a full strike, where they don't), but the employer suffers losses because output drops sharply. It's a calculated squeeze on the employer's production and profits.
Who Takes Part and How It Works

A go-slow is always a collective action — meaning a group of workers does it together, not just one individual. It is usually organized by a trade union (a workers' organization) or agreed upon informally among a workforce.

In practice, during a go-slow, workers might:

  • Take longer breaks than scheduled (but not obvious enough to get fired for).
  • Work at the minimum pace possible while technically still doing their job.
  • Slow down every single step of a process just enough to frustrate output without giving the employer a clear reason to dismiss them.

The cleverness of a go-slow is that workers remain technically on the job. This makes it harder for employers to take disciplinary action, because the workers can argue they are still fulfilling their duties — just not at full speed.
How It Differs from a Strike

This is the most important distinction to understand clearly.

Go-SlowStrike

In a strike, workers refuse to work at all. They walk out, picket outside the building, and the employer's operations can grind to a complete halt. However, striking workers typically earn no wages during this period, which means they bear a real personal financial cost.

In a go-slow, workers remain on the job and continue to be paid. The financial pain falls mostly on the employer, whose production drops but whose wage bill stays the same (or close to it). This makes a go-slow a less risky option for workers who cannot afford to lose their income but still want to exert pressure.

While "go-slow" is most commonly used in the context of labor and industrial disputes, it can also be used more generally to describe any deliberate policy of doing something slowly or cautiously — even outside the workplace.

For example:

  • "The government's go-slow on implementing the new policy frustrated reform groups."

Here, "go-slow" means the government was intentionally dragging its feet and not moving forward at the speed people expected or wanted. This broader usage follows the same spirit as the original meaning: a deliberate, intentional slowing down — not accidental laziness, but a calculated choice to move slowly.

The single most important thing to remember about a go-slow is that it is always deliberate. It is not about workers being naturally slow, tired, or incompetent. It is a conscious, planned, and often coordinated decision to reduce the pace of work as a tool of protest or pressure. That intentionality is what gives the word its meaning and its power.

Imagine nurses at a hospital are unhappy about low pay and demand a raise. Their union tells them not to strike (because patients need care), but to carry out a go-slow instead. So the nurses take longer between tasks, move more slowly through their routines, and take their full allocated break times to the minute — things they might normally rush through. The hospital's efficiency drops. Patient waiting times increase. Management feels the pressure. Negotiations begin.

That is a go-slow.
6953:
When you call something your "go-to," you mean it is your most trusted, most relied-upon choice for a specific purpose — the one you reach for first, almost automatically, because you know it works.

Here's a simple mental image: imagine you have a drawer full of pens, but there's always one you grab. Not because it's the prettiest, but because it writes smoothly every time and never lets you down. That pen is your "go-to" pen. You don't compare it against the others every time. You just reach for it.

The word quietly packs in three ideas at once.

First, it's your first choice, not your second. A go-to option is where your mind goes immediately when a need arises. You don't sit down and weigh all the options. You just... go to it. That instant, instinctive movement toward something is exactly what the word is capturing.

Second, it's proven. You don't call something go-to after using it once. It earns that label because it has worked again and again. There is quiet, accumulated trust built into the word — trust that comes from experience.

Third, it's go-to for a specific purpose. Your go-to friend for emotional support might be a completely different person from your go-to friend for a fun night out. Your go-to tool for cooking might have nothing to do with your go-to app for work. That specificity is always there, even when it isn't said out loud.

Almost anything. A person can be go-to: "She's my go-to when I need honest feedback" — meaning you trust her above others for that purpose. A place can be go-to: "That café is my go-to spot for studying" — it reliably gives you the right environment. A thing can be go-to: "Ibuprofen is my go-to for headaches" — it works, you trust it, you reach for it first. Even a strategy or move can be go-to: "His go-to tactic in negotiations is to stay silent and let the other person talk" — a reliable technique he uses when he needs it most.
How it works in a sentence

"Go-to" always comes before the noun it describes, and it is always hyphenated: "my go-to restaurant," "the go-to solution," "her go-to strategy." You'll almost always see it paired with a possessive — "my," "his," "her," "their," "our," or "the" — because "go-to" is fundamentally about who is doing the relying.

"My go-to" tells you that you are the one relying on it. "The go-to" (using "the") signals that many people in a given context rely on it — it's the widely recognized trusted option, not just one person's private preference: "She's the go-to lawyer in town for property disputes."

This is where precision really matters.

Go-to vs. favorite: Your favorite is what you love most — it's emotional and personal. Your go-to is what you rely on most — it's practical and functional. These two can overlap, but they don't have to. Your favorite restaurant might be somewhere you visit only on special occasions, while your go-to restaurant is the one you drive to on a random Tuesday. The go-to earns its status through performance, not just affection.

Go-to vs. best: "Best" is about quality. "Go-to" is about trust and reliability. The best sushi place in your city might be expensive and hard to book — so it's not your go-to. Your go-to sushi place is the one you reach easily, without planning, and it never disappoints. Quality and go-to status often overlap, but not always.

Go-to vs. default: A default often carries a subtle sense of settling — you end up there when nothing else is available or when you can't be bothered to think. A go-to is a positive, deliberate, trusted choice. You actively choose your go-to; you merely fall back on your default.
Register: Where you'll find this word

"Go-to" is casual and informal. You'll hear it in everyday conversation and read it in blogs, interviews, and social media. It would feel out of place in formal academic writing or legal documents. In everyday speech and informal writing, however, it's very common.

"Go-to" is always positive or neutral — you would never use it to describe something bad or unreliable, because that would contradict the word's very meaning. Also, go-to status isn't permanent. If your go-to restaurant closes down or your go-to person moves away, you'll naturally find a new one — the label belongs to whoever or whatever currently holds that trusted, first-choice role. And finally, something can be your go-to in one area while being completely irrelevant in another, because the word is always tied to a specific context or need.
6954: A goad is something that pushes or forces a person (or animal) into action — usually action they would not have taken on their own, and often through pressure, pain, or irritation.

1. The Literal Meaning (a physical object)

In its original, concrete sense, a goad is a long, pointed stick — traditionally used by farmers and cattle herders to poke livestock (like oxen or cattle) to make them move. When an animal is slow, stubborn, or refusing to budge, the herdsman pokes it with this sharp stick. The animal feels a sting, and moves.

Think of it this way: it is not a gentle tap. It is a deliberate, sharp prod designed to get results through discomfort.

2. The Figurative Meaning (an idea, feeling, or circumstance)

This is the more common and more powerful usage. Here, a goad is anything — a feeling, a situation, a remark, a memory, a threat — that provokes or drives a person into action, especially when they are hesitant, unwilling, or at rest.

Just like the sharp stick moves a stubborn animal, a goad in this sense moves a person — it stirs them, unsettles them, and compels them to do something.
The All-Important Feeling Behind the Word

This is what separates "goad" from a simple word like "reason" or "motivation." A goad carries a quality of pressure, discomfort, or urgency. It is rarely pleasant. It is the kind of thing that nags at you, pricks your conscience, or irritates you into movement.

It is not the reason you want to act. It is the reason you have to act — or feel you cannot stay still any longer.
Examples That Show the Word in Action

• "Hunger was the goad that drove him to finally look for work." (He didn't want to look for work, but hunger left him no choice.)
  • "Her mocking words were a constant goad to his pride." (Her insults stung him and kept pushing him to prove her wrong.)
  • "The fear of failure was the only goad keeping him awake through the night." (Not enthusiasm — fear. That discomfort was what kept him going.)
  • "Poverty can be a powerful goad to ambition." (The pain and pressure of poverty forces some people to strive harder.)
What Makes a Goad Different from Similar Words?

WordWhat it suggests
IncentiveSomething attractive that pulls you toward action (a reward, a bonus)
MotiveA reason — neutral, could be positive or negative
GoadSomething that pushes you, often through discomfort or pressure — more forceful and less pleasant than an incentive

An incentive attracts you toward action — it is something you want. A motive is simply a reason — neutral in tone. But a goad pushes you — often uncomfortably. You don't move because it feels good; you move because staying still feels worse. That edge of discomfort or pressure is what makes "goad" its own distinct word.
The Single Clearest Way to Remember It

A goad is anything that pokes you into action — just like a sharp stick pokes a stubborn ox.

Whether it is guilt, fear, insult, desperation, ambition, or circumstance — if it drives you forward through pressure rather than pleasure, it is a goad.

"Goad" is a moderately forceful word. It implies something more than a mild nudge — it suggests real pressure. But it does not necessarily mean violence or cruelty. It simply means the driving force was sharp enough to actually move someone who might otherwise have stayed put.

It is used in formal writing, literature, and thoughtful speech. You will rarely hear it in casual conversation, but you will see it often in essays, novels, speeches, and journalism — whenever a writer wants to describe what compelled a person to act under pressure.
6955:
To goad someone means to pressure, provoke, or push them into doing something — especially something they are reluctant to do, or something they end up doing out of frustration, anger, or wounded pride.

Think of it this way: imagine someone poking you repeatedly with a stick — not hard enough to seriously hurt you, but persistently enough that you finally snap and react. That "poking" — whether literal or through words, taunts, or challenges — is what goading captures perfectly.
The Full Meaning, Layer by Layer

1. The Basic Action

When you goad someone, you are not simply asking or requesting. You are applying a kind of pressure that wears the other person down, pushes their buttons, or provokes a reaction out of them. The person being goaded often ends up doing something they wouldn't have done on their own.

His friends goaded him into jumping off the bridge into the river, even though he was terrified.

He didn't want to jump. But the pressure — the taunting, the daring, the "come on, don't be a coward" — pushed him to do it anyway. That's goading.

2. The Mechanism — How Goading Works

People are goaded in a few distinct ways:

  • Through taunts and mockery — someone mocks you, calls you a coward, or challenges your ego until you feel you have to respond.
  • Through persistent nagging — someone keeps pushing and pushing until you finally give in just to make it stop.
  • Through provocation — someone deliberately irritates or angers you until you react, sometimes out of pure frustration.
  • Through challenging someone's pride — implying someone isn't brave, strong, or capable enough to do something, which stings enough to make them act.

3. The Result

The action that results from goading is often:

  • Something the person resisted doing at first
  • Something done out of anger, frustration, or wounded pride rather than calm decision-making
  • Sometimes something the person regrets afterward

She was goaded into shouting at her boss — which she would never have done if he hadn't kept provoking her all morning.

Goad almost always carries a negative or manipulative feel. The person doing the goading is typically seen as the aggressor — they are deliberately stirring someone up, often for selfish reasons or amusement. It's not a neutral word.

That said, occasionally it's used in a more neutral or even positive sense — like a coach goading a player into performing better — but even then, the method involves pressure and provocation rather than kindness.
How It's Used in a Sentence

"Goad" follows a few very common patterns:

Pattern 1: goad + someone + into + (doing) something

They goaded him into starting a fight.
She was goaded into making a rash decision.

Pattern 2: goad + someone + on
(meaning to urge or push someone to continue or go further)

The crowd goaded the boxer on as he kept throwing punches.

Pattern 3: goaded by + (something)
(driven into action by a feeling or force)

Goaded by frustration, he finally slammed the door and left.
Goaded by jealousy, she said things she didn't mean.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Many words are close in meaning to "goad" — but each has a slightly different flavor:

  • Persuade — you convince someone using reason and logic. Goading skips reason and goes straight for the emotions.
  • Encourage — warm and supportive. Goading is pressuring and provocative.
  • Provoke — very close to goad, but "provoke" focuses more on triggering a reaction (like anger), while "goad" focuses more on pushing someone toward a specific action.
  • Egg on — an informal phrase that means almost exactly the same as goad — urging someone to do something risky or unwise through peer pressure or taunting.
  • Needle — to irritate someone persistently with small jabs of criticism or sarcasm. Needling is one common method of goading.
  • Taunt — to mock or challenge someone cruelly. Taunting is often the tool used when goading someone.

So you might say: He taunted and needled her — essentially goading her into reacting.
A Few More Examples to Cement It

• The older boys goaded the younger one into stealing from the shop, knowing he'd be the one to get caught.
  • He had no intention of arguing, but she kept goading him until he finally snapped.
  • The general goaded his soldiers into action by questioning their courage in front of their peers.
  • She felt she'd been goaded into quitting her job — the manager had made her work life so unbearable that it was clearly intentional.
  • Don't let them goad you into doing something you'll regret.

To goad is to deliberately provoke, pressure, or push someone — through taunts, challenges, irritation, or persistent pressure — until they do something they were reluctant to do, often out of anger, hurt pride, or sheer frustration.
6956: The word goat has several distinct meanings. Each one is separate from the others — you use context to figure out which meaning applies.

A goat is a medium-sized, four-legged animal with hooves, a short tail, and usually a pair of horns (both males and females can have them). Many males also grow a small beard. Goats are known for being curious, stubborn, and remarkably good at climbing — they can balance on very steep rocks and hillsides.

Domesticated goats have lived alongside humans for thousands of years and are raised all over the world, especially in Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. Humans keep them for:

  • Milk — Goat milk is used to make cheese (like feta and chèvre), yogurt, and butter.
  • Meat — Commonly eaten in many parts of the world.
  • Fiber — Certain breeds produce high-quality wool-like fiber. Cashmere comes from the Kashmir goat, and mohair comes from the Angora goat.
  • Leather — Goat skin is used to make gloves, shoes, and bookbindings.

Goats are closely related to sheep, but they're quite different in personality — goats are more independent, adventurous, and mischievous, while sheep tend to follow each other and stay calm.

Names for different goats:

  • A male goat is called a buck or a billy (or billy goat).
  • A female goat is called a doe or a nanny (or nanny goat).
  • A baby goat is called a kid.
  • A castrated male goat is called a wether.

Wild goats also exist. The ibex (a wild goat with enormous curved horns) and the mountain goat (found in the Rocky Mountains of North America) are well-known wild relatives.

In mythology and religion, goats have strong symbolic meaning. In Christian imagery, goats are sometimes associated with sinfulness or the devil, which is the opposite of the sheep, which symbolizes innocence. In ancient Greek religion, the god Pan had the legs and horns of a goat. In many cultures, a goat was a common sacrificial animal.

This is a modern, informal use of the word, written either as GOAT (all caps, to show it's an acronym) or simply as goat in casual writing and speech.

When you call someone a GOAT, you are saying they are the single greatest person who has ever lived in their field — better than everyone who came before them and everyone alive today. It is the highest possible compliment.

This term is used most heavily in sports but has spread to music, film, fashion, business, and more.

Examples of how it's used:

  • "Michael Jordan is the GOAT of basketball."
  • "Serena Williams is the GOAT of women's tennis."
  • "People argue endlessly about who the GOAT of cricket is."
  • "That album is a GOAT-level record." (meaning it's of the greatest-of-all-time quality)

You can also use it as a verb informally: "He GOATed that performance" means he performed at an all-time-great level. But as a noun, "the GOAT" or simply "a GOAT" refers to the person or thing considered the greatest ever.
3. The Person Who Causes a Loss or Failure (informal)

This is the opposite of the GOAT meaning above, and it specifically appears in sports contexts (though it can appear elsewhere too).

When a player makes a critical mistake — misses the deciding penalty kick, drops a ball in the final moment, makes the error that costs the team the championship — they are sometimes called "the goat" of the game. It means: the person most responsible for the defeat.

Example:

  • "After missing that penalty, he went from being the hero to being the goat of the match."

This meaning comes from the word scapegoat — a scapegoat is someone who is blamed for the failures of others (it comes from an ancient ritual where a goat was symbolically loaded with the community's sins and sent into the wilderness). Over time, "goat" on its own took on this meaning of "the one who gets the blame."

Important note: In casual conversation, the context tells you which meaning is intended. "He's the GOAT!" is a compliment. "He was the goat of the game" (lowercase, and referring to a loss) is a criticism.

The phrase old goat is a mild, informal insult used to describe a grumpy, unpleasant, or lecherous (overly interested in sex) old man. It has a mocking, dismissive tone.

Examples:

  • "Don't mind him — he's just a grumpy old goat."
  • "The old goat pinched my cheek and wouldn't leave me alone."

It is rarely used for women. It is insulting but not severely so — more playfully rude than deeply offensive.

In astrology, the zodiac sign Capricorn (December 22 – January 19) is symbolized by a sea-goat — a mythical creature that is half goat, half fish. People often simply call Capricorn "the goat."

Example:

  • "She's a Capricorn, so she's the goat of the zodiac — hardworking and ambitious."

This use is casual and comes up in conversations about horoscopes and astrology.

Even when used in idioms, goat still functions as a noun. Here are the most important ones:

  • "Get someone's goat" — To irritate or annoy someone deeply.
    "The way he keeps interrupting really gets my goat."
    (Origin: possibly from a horse-racing tradition, but used today as a general idiom.)
  • "Separate the sheep from the goats" — To distinguish the good, capable, or worthy people from the bad, incapable, or unworthy ones.
    "The final exam will separate the sheep from the goats."
    (From the Bible, where God separates the righteous from the unrighteous at the Last Judgment.)
  • "Act/play the goat" (mainly British English) — To behave in a silly or foolish way.
    "Stop playing the goat and take this seriously."

MeaningWhat it meansExample

To quickly recap: goat primarily means the farm animal. In modern informal English, GOAT (or goat) means the greatest of all time. In sports, goat (lowercase) can also mean the person blamed for a loss. Old goat is a mild insult for an unpleasant elderly man. And in astrology, the goat refers to Capricorn.

The context — who is speaking, what they're talking about, and whether it sounds like a compliment or a criticism — will almost always tell you which meaning is being used.
6957:
A goatee is a style of facial hair where a man grows hair specifically on his chin — and only the chin — while keeping the rest of his face (cheeks, jawline, neck) clean-shaved.

Think of it as a small, neat patch of beard sitting right at the tip of the chin. It is much smaller and more focused than a full beard, which covers the cheeks and jawline too.

Picture a man's face. Now imagine drawing a small oval or circle around just his chin — roughly the area below his lower lip and above the bottom of his chin. The hair growing within that zone is the goatee. The rest of the face stays shaved smooth.

The goatee can be short and stubby or longer and more pointed. A pointed goatee — where the chin hair tapers to a point at the bottom — is a very classic, recognizable version of the style.
The strict meaning vs. everyday usage

Here is something important to know, because this word is used in two slightly different ways:

Strictly speaking, a goatee means only the chin hair, with no mustache. Just the chin, nothing above the upper lip.

In everyday modern usage, however, many people use "goatee" to describe a style that includes both a chin beard and a mustache, where the two are connected — forming a ring or frame around the mouth. This combined style is technically called a circle beard or full goatee, but because people loosely call it a goatee, you will hear the word used both ways.

So when someone says "goatee," they usually mean one of these two things:

  • Chin hair only, no mustache (the original, strict meaning)
  • Chin hair plus a connected mustache (the loose, popular modern meaning)
How it is different from similar styles

It helps to compare it with nearby terms:

  • A beard covers a much wider area — the cheeks, jaw, chin, and neck. A goatee is far smaller and limited to the chin.
  • A mustache is hair grown above the upper lip, under the nose. A goatee is below — on the chin. The two are in completely different locations.
  • A stubble or five o'clock shadow is a thin layer of unshaved hair spread across the entire lower face, not deliberately shaped into a specific zone like a goatee.
  • A Van Dyke (another beard style) looks very similar to a goatee — it has both a chin beard and a mustache — but the key difference is that in a Van Dyke, the mustache and chin beard are separate and do not connect at the corners of the mouth. In a full goatee (circle beard), they do connect.

Goatees are a popular choice for men who want facial hair but prefer a cleaner, more sculpted look rather than a full beard. They require regular shaving and trimming to keep the borders sharp. The style has been associated with artists, musicians, and in popular culture, is sometimes used as a visual shorthand to suggest a "villainous" or mysterious character — you may have noticed that movie and TV villains, or the "evil twin" version of a character, are often depicted with a goatee.
As a noun — how the word is used

Since you asked about the noun form specifically:

  • "He grew a goatee over the summer." — referring to the beard style itself
  • "That actor is known for his goatee." — referring to the specific facial hair on that person
  • "He trimmed his goatee." — the patch of chin hair he maintains

The plural is goatees (e.g., "Both brothers had goatees").

A goatee = a small beard on the chin, with the rest of the face shaved. In strict usage, no mustache. In common usage, sometimes includes a connected mustache too. It is a deliberate, shaped style — not just unshaved growth — and it is distinct from a full beard, a mustache, or stubble.
6958:
To gobble something means to eat it extremely fast and in large amounts, usually without any care for manners. Think of someone who is very hungry (or very greedy) — they don't chew properly, they don't pause, they barely breathe. They just shove food in, one big mouthful after another, until it's gone. That is gobbling.

He gobbled his entire meal in under two minutes.
The kids gobbled their pizza before the adults had even sat down.

Notice that "gobble" doesn't just mean "eat fast." It also carries the idea of greediness or eagerness. A person who gobbles isn't just in a hurry — they want it all, and they want it now. This is what makes "gobble" more vivid and expressive than simply saying "eat quickly."

"Gobble" is very commonly used with the words up or down, forming what are called phrasal verbs. These don't change the meaning much — they just make it feel more complete or emphatic.

  • Gobble up — to eat something entirely and eagerly.
  • Gobble down — same idea, with a slight emphasis on the downward action of swallowing fast.

She gobbled up every last crumb on the plate.
He gobbled down his breakfast and ran out the door.

Both are correct and natural. Native speakers use them interchangeably in casual conversation.

"Gobble" isn't only used for eating. It is also used figuratively — meaning it can describe anything that is consumed, taken, or used up in a rapid, greedy, or overwhelming way. This is one of the most common uses you'll encounter, so pay close attention.

When a thing uses up resources too fast:

This video game gobbles up a lot of battery.
The new software gobbles down memory like crazy.

When a company or person takes over others quickly:

The giant corporation gobbled up three smaller companies last year.
He gobbled up every available ticket before anyone else had a chance.

When time or money disappears fast:

Rent and bills gobble up most of my salary.
The project gobbled up six months of our time.

In all these cases, the image is the same: something is being consumed eagerly, completely, and with a kind of unstoppable appetite.

"Gobble" has one more, completely separate meaning: the sound a turkey makes. When a turkey makes its loud, bubbling, repetitive call, we say it is gobbling. This is a standalone meaning, unrelated to eating or consuming.

The turkeys in the yard started gobbling as soon as we walked near them.

This meaning is used specifically and only for turkeys. You will see and hear it, especially around Thanksgiving in American culture, so it's worth knowing — but it won't come up very often in everyday conversation.

"Gobble" is an informal, expressive, and slightly humorous word. It is perfectly correct English, but it belongs to casual speech and writing rather than formal writing. You would use it in a text to a friend, in a story, in everyday conversation, or in informal articles. You would not typically use it in a formal business report or an academic paper.

It also often carries a mildly negative or teasing tone when used about people — describing someone as gobbling their food is a gentle way of saying they lack table manners, or are being hilariously greedy.

Stop gobbling — the food isn't going anywhere!

1. To eat very fast and greedily — the core, most common meaning.
2. To consume, take, or use up something rapidly and eagerly — the figurative extension of meaning #1, used for time, money, battery, companies, opportunities, etc.
3. (Of a turkey) to make its characteristic loud call — a separate, specific meaning.

Once you understand that the heart of "gobble" is this image of something being hungrily swallowed up — fast, completely, and with great appetite — both the literal and figurative uses will feel natural and obvious to you every time you encounter the word.
6959:
Gobbledygook is language — spoken or written — that is so confusing, so unnecessarily complicated, or so full of meaningless words that it becomes almost impossible to understand. When you call something gobbledygook, you are saying it communicates little to nothing, even though it may look or sound like it's saying something important.

It is always a criticism. Nobody ever says "what beautiful gobbledygook." The word is dismissive and a little mocking.

The word covers two slightly different but closely related ideas, and you will encounter both in real life.

The first is overcomplicated language that has a meaning buried inside it, but that meaning has been so smothered in jargon, long-winded phrases, and unnecessary complexity that ordinary people cannot extract it. Think of a legal contract filled with phrases like "hereinafter referred to as the aforementioned party of the first part" when it simply means "you." The information is technically in there, but it has been dressed up so heavily that it stops functioning as communication.

The second is language that is essentially pure noise — strings of words that sound official or intelligent but don't actually mean anything coherent at all.
